items.question: Why do you think it has become so difficult to create good benchmarks for world models and text-based models?
items.object: Benchmarking world models and text-based models
items.answer: I think this whole space is extremely difficult as things are emerging now. And I mean, it's not only for world models, I think it's for everything, including text-based models, right? In the early days, it seemed very easy to have good benchmarks because we could do things like question-answering benchmarks. But these days, so much of what people are wanting to do is nothing like that, right? You're wanting to get some recommendations about which backpack would be best for you for your trip in Europe next month. It's not so easy to come up with a benchmark. And it's the same problem with these world models.

And it's the same problem with these world models.

rubrics.text: The response attributes the difficulty of creating good model benchmarks to a mismatch between conventional question-answering tasks and what users increasingly want models to do.

items.question: How do you see Moonlake's approach to visual understanding fitting into the broader pursuit of artificial intelligence?
items.object: Moonlake's approach to visual understanding
items.answer: The overall goal is the pursuit of artificial intelligence, and most of my career's been doing that in the language space. That's been just extremely productive, as we all know from the story of the last few years. I don't have to tell you about how much we've achieved with large language models. But although they're being extremely effective for ramping language and general intelligence, it's clearly not the whole world. There's this multimodal world of vision, sound, taste that you'd like to be dealing with more than just language. And then the question is how to do it. Despite a huge investment in the computer vision space—computer vision has been a research field for decades, far, far larger than the language space—I think it's fair to say that vision understanding sort of stalled out. You got to object recognition and then progress just wasn't being made. If you look at any of these vision-language models, it's the language that's doing 90% of the work and the vision barely works. So there's really an interesting research question as to why that is. At heart, the ideas behind Moonlake are an attempt to answer that, believing that there can be a really rich connection between a more symbolic layer of abstracted understanding of visual domains, which aren't in the mainstream vision models, which are still trying to operate on the surface level of pixels.

items.question: How do you distinguish an action-conditioned world model from a generative AI video model?
items.object: Action-conditioned world models and spatial intelligence
items.answer: I think this is actually a little bit subtle because people look at these amazing generative AI video models or VO3 or these things, and they think Genies. They think, “Oh, this is amazing. This is sort of, you know, we've solved understanding the world because you can produce these generative AI videos.” But the reality is that although the visuals do look fantastic, those visuals actually aren't accompanied by an understanding of the 3D world, understanding how objects can move, what the consequences of different actions are, and that's what's really needed for spatial intelligence. A term we sometimes use is that you need action-conditioned world models: you only actually have a world model if you can predict, given some action is taken, what is going to change in the world because of it. In particular, that becomes hard over longer time scales. If you're simply trying to predict the next video frame, that's not so difficult. But what you actually want to do is understand the likely consequences of actions minutes into the future. To do that, you need much more of an abstracted semantic model of the world.

items.question: How do you assess the idea that collecting enough observational video data will produce a world model that understands the consequences of actions?
items.object: Observational video data for learning action-conditioned world models
items.answer: One possibility is, look, if we just collect masses and masses and masses and masses of video data, this problem will be solved. Under certain assumptions, that could be true. But there are multiple avenues in which it could not be true. The first is, what's really essential is understanding the consequences of actions, producing an action-conditioned world model. If you're simply collecting observational video data, which is the easy stuff to collect when you're mining online videos, you don't actually know the actions that are being taken to see how the video is changing. If you're never collecting actions directly, and you're having to try and infer them from what happened in the observed video, that's not impossible, but it's very hard. It's not really established that you can get that to work at any scale yet. There's a lot of premium on collecting action-conditioned video data, which is part of why there's been a lot of interest in using simulation, so that you can be collecting data where you do know the actions, which is in quite limited supply.

items.question: Why do you think semantic abstractions are the right representation for world models?
items.object: Semantic abstraction as a representation for world models
items.answer: In the limit of as much data as you could possibly have, maybe the problem is eventually solvable. Even though we collect huge amounts of text data, text data is always at a great level of abstraction, right? Language is a human-designed abstracted representation, where there's meaning in each token, and it's representing an abstraction of the world. As soon as you're describing someone as a professor, and as soon as you're saying that they're condescending, these are very abstracted descriptions of the world. It's not at what you're observing as pixel level. To get to that kind of degree of abstraction starting from pixels is orders of magnitude of extra data and processing. Although we absolutely want to exploit, get as much data as possible, use the bitter lesson, nevertheless, if there are ways in which you can work with five orders of magnitude less data than people working purely from pixels, you're going to be able to make a lot more progress a lot more quickly. And that's the bit here. You could just say that's only wanting to be able to do it more efficiently, more quickly, more cheaply. But I think it's actually more than that. I think one should be making the analogy to how human beings work. At one level, yes, we have these high-resolution eyes and we can look and see a scene like a video. But all of the evidence from neuroscience and psychology is that most of what comes into people's eyes is never processed. You're doing fairly fine-grained processing of exactly what you're focusing on. But as soon as it's away from that, “Yeah, there's another guy over there,” you're only processing top-down this very abstracted semantic description of the world around you. That's what human beings are doing. They're working with semantic abstractions. I think it is just the right representation because we also have other goals. We want to be able to do real-time worlds. That means there's a limit to how much process you can do. And we want to do long-term planning and consistency. Again, that favors abstraction.

items.question: How do you view storing text rather than pixels to maintain a long-term memory of what's happening in the world?
items.object: Text versus pixel-level representations for long-term world memory
items.answer: To maintain a long-term memory of what's happening in the world so we can do longer term, we're actually storing text of what has been happening in the world, right? It's not such a successful strategy of trying to keep it all at a pixel level.
quotes: To maintain a long-term memory of what's happening in the world so we can do longer term, we're actually storing text of what has been happening in the world, right? It's not such a successful strategy of trying to keep it all at a pixel level.

rubrics.text: The response judges storing the entire history of world events at the pixel level to be a relatively ineffective strategy for long-term memory.

items.question: How do you differ from Yann LeCun in your understanding of the role of language and symbolic representations in intelligence?
items.object: Language and symbolic representations in intelligence and Moonlake’s world models
items.answer: Yann LeCun is a dear friend of mine, but he has never appreciated the power of language in particular or symbolic representations in general. Yann is a very visual thinker. He always wants to claim that he thinks visually and there are no word symbols or math in his head. Maybe that's true of Yann, and it's certainly not the way I think. But anyway, the world according to Yann is that the basic stuff of the world and of intelligence is visual, and language is just this low-bit-rate communication mechanism between humans, and it doesn't have much other utility and it's far inferior to the high-bit-rate video that comes into your eyes. I think he's fundamentally missing a number of important things there. Think of this evolutionary argument looking at animals. The closest analogy is the things with chimps. Chimpanzees have fairly similar brains to human beings. They have great vision systems. They have great memory systems. They've got better memory than we do of short-term memories. They can plan. They can build primitive tools. But humans are massively ahead in what we understand about the world, what we can plan, what we can build. Essentially, what took off for us was that humans managed to develop language. That gave a symbolic knowledge representation and reasoning level which just gave this sort of vaulting of what could be done with the intelligence in brains. The philosopher Dan Dennett refers to language as a cognitive tool and argues that humans, unique among the creatures in the world, have managed to build their own cognitive tools. Language is the famous first example, but other things like mathematics and programming languages are also cognitive tools. They give you an ability to think in abstractions, in extended causal reasoning chains. That allows you to do much more. We use that for spatial representation and intelligence and planning and gameplay as well. We believe, and this is underlying the specific technologies that Moonlake is making, that symbolic representations are powerful and you want to use them in your understanding of the visual world when you want a causal understanding, when you want to maintain long-term consistency and prediction. As I understand it, that's just not in Yann LeCun's worldview. I think that's a fundamental philosophical difference.

items.question: How do you assess Yann LeCun’s JEPA as a direction for building models of the visual world?
items.object: Yann LeCun’s JEPA model
items.answer: That's a reasonable research bet as a direction to head for building out a model of the visual world. To my mind, it's one reasonable research bet; it's not really established that it's the best one that everyone should be following.

items.question: How do you assess Yann LeCun’s argument that autoregressive language models cannot provide the joint representation needed for a consistent world model?
items.object: Yann LeCun’s argument that autoregressive language models cannot provide a joint world representation
items.answer: I think there's a part of JEPA that's right, which is you do want to have a joint embedding that gives you a consistent model of the world. Yann's argument is you can never get that from autoregressive language models because they're sort of left-to-right churning out one token at a time. I guess this is where we're in the research arguments of the field. I'm not actually convinced that's right because although the token production is this autoregressive process that's heading left to right, I guess it doesn't have to be left to right. Anyway, in a sequence of tokens, we could have right-to-left Arabic. Although that's true, all of the weights of the model that are internal to the transformer, they are a joint model of the model's understanding of the world. I think you can think of the weights of the model as a form of joint representation, and therefore, it is plausible to think that that could be the basis of a world model which avoids Yann's objections.

items.question: Why do you see building a world model around an abstract semantic world state, with diffusion generating the graphics on top, as a better path?
items.object: World modeling with an abstract semantic world state and diffusion-generated graphics
items.answer: The difference is, and Sun was pointing at this, where he's sort of saying it's in one way a more difficult path, but a better path: typically the diffusion models are producing the whole scene and it looks lovely, but there isn't spatial understanding behind it, which is allowing for the real-time graphics gameplay, the spatial intelligence, understanding the consequences of worlds. This is taking a path where it is assuming an abstracted semantic model of the world, the world state, and then the diffusion model is being used on top of that to produce the high-quality graphics.

items.question: How do you think language models and world models should be evaluated as people use them for increasingly complex tasks?
items.object: Evaluating language models and world models on real user tasks
items.answer: I think this whole space is extremely difficult as things are emerging now. I mean, it's not only for world models. I think it's for everything, including text-based models, right? In the early days, it seemed very easy to have good benchmarks because we could do things like question-answering benchmarks: could you answer the question based on these documents? And the various other kinds of, you know, do pieces of logical reasoning or math. But again, they're sort of visual equivalents of things like object recognition, right? They're these small component tasks. These days, so much of what people are wanting to do also with language models is nothing like that, right? You're wanting to have an interaction with a language model and get some recommendations about which backpack would be best for you for your trip in Europe next month. It's not so easy to come up with a benchmark as to whether this large language model gives you an effective interaction for guiding you in a good way for shopping, right? It's the same problem with these world models. If we take the game design case, success is that a game designer can produce what they are imagining in a reasonable amount of time. That's really the kind of macro task. But that's a very hard thing to turn into a benchmark. I think a lot of this is actually going to turn into people walking with their feet. I guess that's what's happening at the large language model level, right? When people are choosing to use GPT-5 or Gemini or Claude, individuals are trying out these different models and deciding, “Oh, I like the kind of answers that GPT-5 gives me,” or, “No, I feel like I get more accurate detail from Claude.” It's a lot of people just using it. People feel it's giving them utility in what they want, right?

items.question: How do you weigh visual quality against gameplay when judging a world model for games?
items.object: Visual quality versus gameplay in world models for games
items.answer: I think that's a really important distinction for speaking to Moonlake's strength. Great visuals are lovely to look at for a few seconds, but games are really all about the concept, the gameplay, and a lot of the time that doesn't even require great visuals. There are lots of very successful games which have relatively primitive visuals, and there are other games where people have spent millions producing photorealistic visuals, and the game sucks. Keeping those two axes apart is really important in thinking about what's important in a world model for different uses.

items.question: How do you assess the usefulness of video generation models as world simulators?
items.object: Video generation models as world simulators
items.answer: The point I'm trying to make is that there are very many different types of world simulators. Having a world simulator that can produce pixel coherency is very useful for games and marketing and all these things. But it's not as useful as people think when it comes to causal reasoning, when it comes to embodied AI. We're not saying that it's not a great world simulator, but the bet is more so that there's going to be a disproportionately large share of value of real-world tasks and virtual tasks where high-resolution pixel fidelity is not needed. Video models have their value.

But it's not as useful as people think when it comes to causal reasoning, when it comes to embodied AI.

items.answer: I would also make the observation that as the AAA games industry has developed, the line between what is a movie and what is a game has blurred. You do end up basically producing a two-hour movie.
quotes: I would also make the observation that as the AAA games industry has developed, the line between what is a movie and what is a game has blurred. You do end up basically producing a two-hour movie.

items.question: What do you find compelling about giving AI agents tools and abstractions that can produce capabilities such as spatial audio?
items.object: Emergent capabilities from giving AI agents tools and abstractions
items.answer: We're giving our model an abstraction or a suite of tools such that it's able to achieve that. You can argue that spatial is an emergence out of the tools and abstraction that we provide to the agents. I think that's the beauty of this approach. There's a lot of things, kind of like how humanity's built technology, and they're like LEGO blocks that build on top of each other. It's the same thing here. There are going to be things that sort of emerge from being able to put these things together in combinatorially interesting ways.

items.question: How did you come to move from language research toward visual understanding and world models?
items.object: The move from language research toward visual understanding and world models
items.answer: To some extent, the answer is the enthusiasm and creativity of students. But there's a bit of a history there. Clearly most of my career has been doing stuff with language. How I got into research was thinking, “Ah, this is just so amazing how humans can produce speech and understand each other in real time. Somehow they manage to learn languages when they're kids. How could this possibly happen?” Starting off, I was very focused on language. As it got into the 2010s, I had been working on question answering, and then I started to get interested in visual question answering. That was an area where it was very noticeable that the visual understanding was bad. These were the days when it seemed like there was almost no visual understanding. You were just getting answers that came from priors. If you asked how many people are sitting at the table, it'd always answer two regardless of how many people you could see in the picture. It seemed like these models actually aren't able to get semantic information out of images. I was interested in that problem and tried to work more on that, and that required knowing more about what's happening in vision and how you can represent visual information. Then things started to be this revolution of doing generative AI images, and I had students that started looking at that. Before Moonlake, I was also working with Demi Guo, who founded Pika.

items.question: How do you look back on the joint language-vision research you were doing when Richard Socher and Andrej Karpathy were PhD students?
items.object: Early joint language-vision research during Richard Socher and Andrej Karpathy’s PhD years
items.answer: There were several papers in that era. Andrej Karpathy was a PhD student at the same time as Richard, and so there was some joint language-vision work in that era as well. It seems kind of ancient by modern standards, but we were trying to go from textual dependency graphs to visual scenes.

items.question: What makes Walt Disney one of your favorite founders?
items.object: Walt Disney as a founder
items.answer: Walt Disney is also one of my favorite founders. His story is like, at the time, “Okay, I'm going to create this immersive park.” People don't even have that technology to create it virtually, but, you know what, let's just build it physically so that people can—
